1790: Gobindabhog, Kalonunia, Radhatilak and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so that this attribute cannot determine the selection for the group as a whole.
1797: Consistency describes the textural coherence of the finished dish and the degree to which it corresponds to the requirements of the preparation. In table rice the values ranged from 7.43 in Lal Badshabhog to 8.35 in Radhatilak; against the control at 7.72, 4 cultivars ranked higher, Radhatilak being the highest. Kalojira recorded the highest value in khichdi at 8.51 and Gobindabhog the lowest at 6.88; the control returned 7.02, 6 cultivars exceeded it, Kalojira most markedly. For pulao the values lay between 6.83 and 8.01, with the control at 7.93; here no cultivar exceeded the control and Harinakhuri ranked highest. In payash the values ranged from 6.78 in Kalonunia to 8.41 in Gobindabhog; the control returned 7.13, 2 cultivars exceeded that value and Gobindabhog ranked first. Means for this attribute are set out in Table 4.64 and illustrated in Fig. 4.29.
1798: Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. Year exerted no significant effect, alone or in combination with cultivar, so that the ranking was reproduced. Variation between replicates was small, the coefficient of variation lying between 1.44 and 4.51%. Consistency is contingent upon the degree of starch gelatinisation and subsequent retrogradation, and upon the protein network surrounding the granules.
1799: Published work is concordant. Cheng et al. (2019) determined that heat and moisture yield a firmer, less adhesive network, and Iqbal et al. (2021) reported that firmness follows the starch and protein network. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) observed that texture and colour jointly determine acceptance, and Devi and Badwaik (2022) recorded that texture and pasting behaviour follow amylose content and starch structure. No single cultivar proved superior across all the products: Gobindabhog, Harinakhuri, Kalojira and Radhatilak ranked highest in different ones, so that the decision is contingent upon the product concerned.
1806: Cooking quality summarises water uptake, cooking time and the structural integrity of the cooked grain. Radhatilak recorded the highest value in table rice at 8.42 and Lal Badshabhog the lowest at 7.36; relative to 7.70 for the control, 5 cultivars were higher, Radhatilak ranking best among them. For khichdi the values lay between 7.00 and 8.45, with the control at 7.07; here 7 cultivars exceeded the control, Lal Badshabhog ranking highest. In pulao the values ranged from 5.85 in Lal Badshabhog to 8.28 in Radhunipagal; with the control at 7.08, 6 cultivars exceeded it and Radhunipagal proved the best. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value in payash at 8.18 and Dudeshwar the lowest at 6.80; the control recorded 6.80, 8 cultivars exceeded it and Gobindabhog ranked most favourable. Table 4.65 carries the means, which are plotted in Fig. 4.30. The cultivars differed significantly in every product. Year and its interaction with cultivar both fell short of significance, so that the order was identical in each year. With coefficients of variation of 1.49 to 3.86%, the experiment was well controlled.
1807: Cooking quality is contingent upon gelatinisation temperature, amylose content and the structural integrity of the grain, which is why it tracks alkali spreading value and amylose. Previous reports are concordant. Ayamdoo et al. (2014) demonstrated that cooking behaviour alters progressively with treatment severity, and Kwofie and Ngadi (2017) noted that time and temperature constitute the processor's principal controls. Buggenhout et al. (2013) concluded that cultivar and processing history operate jointly, and Cheng et al. (2019) demonstrated that gelatinisation governs water uptake and cooking time.
1808: The most favourable entry varied between products: Gobindabhog, Lal Badshabhog, Radhatilak and Radhunipagal each ranked highest in one product or another, so that selection is contingent upon the product concerned.
1815: The analysis of variance addresses one attribute at a time, so that a single figure was required to establish which cultivar is superior overall. This was accomplished using the total quality scoring approach of Ismail et al. (2001), in which each attribute is scored, weighted for its importance, and the weighted scores summed. Kraggerud et al. (2012) subsequently examined whether such a score genuinely reflects overall quality and concluded that it does. Here every attribute on which the cultivars differed significantly was placed on a scale of 0 to 100, oriented so that 100 invariably denotes the superior outcome, then averaged within five groups and combined by weight: sensory 30%, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10. The weights constitute a stated convention rather than a property of the data, and the index may be recomputed under any alternative set. The result is given in Table 4.66, and the score of every cultivar in every group appears in Table 4.68.
1819: On this index the superior cultivar was Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for khichdi, Kataribhog for pulao and Gobindabhog for payash. The control ranked at or near the bottom in every product, so that substituting the cultivars named here for Dudeshwar would improve the product without any alteration in the method of preparation. Table 4.67 gives, for each product, the cultivar exhibiting the best balance of attributes relative to the control.
1824: The table below gives the five group scores and the composite score for every cultivar in every product, so that the standing of any entry may be read directly. The weights applied were sensory 30%, nutritional 25, bioactive 20, mineral 15 and colour 10.
1829: The weights above were assigned rather than computed, so the ranking was verified against a second set of weights derived from the data themselves. Principal component analysis was performed on the merit scores, and each attribute was then weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading multiplied by the share of variance that component carries. This constitutes the customary procedure for assigning weights to a composite indicator without recourse to judgement. The two rankings corresponded closely, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.942 and a minimum of 0.867, and the same cultivar ranked first in 3 of the 4 products, as Table 4.69 demonstrates. The ranking therefore proceeds from the data and not from the particular weights adopted. Principal component analysis is employed here solely to assign the weights; the components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, since a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the more desirable.
1833: The mean rank correlation was 0.942 and the minimum 0.867, and the same cultivar ranked first in 3 of the 4 products. The ranking is therefore not an artefact of the weights adopted. Where the two diverged, the cultivars concerned were in any case closely positioned on the index, so that the divergence is one of order between near-equals rather than of substance.
1835: Cluster analysis was employed to examine how the cultivars and the products group together when all the attributes are considered simultaneously. The 40 cultivar and product combinations were standardised on the 22 attributes determined in every product, and Ward's method was applied to the Euclidean distances between them, the number of groups being set at 4. Where a cluster contains only one product, the method of preparation determines the quality profile; where cultivars of different products fall together, the two are comparable in the finished form.
1841: Of the 4 clusters, 3 contain only one product. This indicates that the products differ from one another to a greater extent than the cultivars differ within any one product. Amarnath and Ravi Kumar (2025) applied Ward's method comparably in rice and drew upon the cluster means to select genotypes for further work, on the reasoning that crosses between distant clusters are more likely to generate useful variation. Dutta and Mahanta (2014) advanced the same point from the product side, namely that different traditional preparations require genuinely different raw material.
1843: Nine traditional aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal were evaluated against Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar serving as the control, in the 4 cooked products of this group. Each was grown and prepared identically for two years and analysed as a pooled completely randomised design. In every product the cultivars differed significantly for nearly all the attributes determined, whereas year and its interaction with cultivar were significant for considerably fewer. The principal finding is therefore unambiguous: the choice of cultivar determines the quality of the product, and the year of production is of markedly less consequence. A cultivar selected on one year of results will generally retain its position in the next.
1844: On this index the superior cultivar was Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for khichdi, Kataribhog for pulao and Gobindabhog for payash. The control ranked at or near the bottom in every product, so that substituting the cultivars named here for Dudeshwar would improve the product without any alteration in the method of preparation. Table 4.67 gives, for each product, the cultivar exhibiting the best balance of attributes relative to the control.
1845: The weights above were assigned rather than computed, so the ranking was verified against a second set of weights derived from the data themselves. Principal component analysis was performed on the merit scores, and each attribute was then weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading multiplied by the share of variance that component carries. This is the common procedure for assigning weights to a composite indicator without recourse to judgement. The two rankings corresponded closely, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.942 and a minimum of 0.867, and the same cultivar ranked first in 3 of the 4 products, as Table 4.69 demonstrates. The ranking therefore proceeds from the data and not from the particular weights adopted. Principal component analysis is employed here solely to assign the weights; the components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, since a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the more desirable.
1846: Cluster analysis was then performed on all 40 cultivar and product combinations together, using the 22 attributes determined in every product. Ward's method resolved them into 4 groups, of which 3 contained a single product only (Table 4.70 and Fig. 4.31). When the products are compared with one another, therefore, it is the method of preparation rather than the cultivar that determines the broad quality type, whereas within any one product the cultivar is the variable under the processor's control. The two findings are complementary rather than contradictory: the preparation determines the type of product and the cultivar its standing within that type.
1847: The cultivars identified here should be re-evaluated on a larger scale and over additional years before being recommended generally. For breeding work directed at improving the group as a whole, parents are best drawn from different clusters, since crosses between distant clusters are more likely to release useful variation.
1850: Amylose content determines the firmness and discreteness of the cooked grain: a higher content yields a firmer, drier grain that retains its shape, and a lower content a softer, stickier one. In popped rice the values ranged from 15.66 in Harinakhuri to 19.64% in Kalojira; the control recorded 16.97%, 8 cultivars exceeded it, and Kalojira proved the most favourable. Kalojira recorded the highest value in puffed rice at 19.69% and Harinakhuri the lowest at 15.64%; against 17.38% for the control, 7 cultivars exceeded it, Kalojira being the most favourable entry. For flattened rice the values lay between 16.00 and 20.01%, with the control at 17.61%; Kalonunia ranked first, and 8 cultivars in all exceeded the control. The data are presented in Table 4.71 and plotted in Fig. 4.32.
1851: Cultivars differed significantly in all the products. In 1 products the year effect was significant and in 1 the year × cultivar interaction, the cultivars thus retaining a similar order in both years. The coefficient of variation remained within 0.10 to 0.89%, indicative of good precision. Amylose is deposited by granule-bound starch synthase I at the Waxy locus, and cultivars differ in the allele they carry. Cooking disorganises the granule but does not alter the quantity of amylose present.
1852: Published work is concordant. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) determined that apparent amylose governs eating and processing behaviour, and Tian et al. (2018) reported that crystallinity and digestibility decline without any change in amylose. Cheng et al. (2019) observed that heat and moisture reconstitute the matrix into a firmer gel, and Devi and Badwaik (2022) recorded that amylose accounts for most of the varietal difference in cooking behaviour. The most favourable entry varied between products: Kalojira and Kalonunia each ranked highest in one product or another, so that selection is contingent upon the product concerned.
1859: Starch constitutes the energy-supplying fraction of the grain and the basis of its texture; a higher value indicates a well-filled endosperm and good recovery of the edible fraction. Harinakhuri recorded the highest value in popped rice at 77.07% and Kataribhog the lowest at 73.00%; the control returned 73.11%, 8 cultivars exceeded it, Harinakhuri most markedly. For puffed rice the values lay between 73.85 and 78.50%, with the control at 75.41%; here one cultivar exceeded the control and Harinakhuri ranked highest. In flattened rice the values ranged from 70.22 in Dudeshwar to 74.15% in Harinakhuri; against the control at 70.22%, 8 cultivars ranked higher, Harinakhuri being the highest. Table 4.72 lists the means and Fig. 4.33 presents them graphically. The cultivars differed significantly in every product. Neither year nor the year × cultivar term attained significance, ranking being unchanged between years. Precision was satisfactory, coefficients of variation ranging from 0.31 to 1.41%.
